Objections do not reveal a fundamental flaw in the ensemble calibration; they justify a modest downward recalibration to reflect downside scenarios.

causal-factors.name: Current pace through February 2026
causal-factors.rationale: As of late February 2026, about 606 migrants had died or gone missing in the Mediterranean; continuing March–April at a similar pace would bring the total toward the 1,000 mark before May.

causal-factors.name: Spring crossing season and weather conditions
causal-factors.rationale: Historical patterns show higher mortality risk during the spring crossing window due to more crossings and shifting sea conditions.

causal-factors.name: Historical annual toll context (roughly 2,000–2,500 deaths per year)
causal-factors.rationale: Annual Mediterranean death tolls in recent years are in the low-to-mid thousands, making a 1,000-death milestone by April not outside the realm of plausibility.

causal-factors.name: Data completeness and missing/unverified cases
causal-factors.rationale: IOM data include missing or unverified counts; additional unverified cases could push the total higher than currently documented.

causal-factors.name: Proximity to threshold and timeframe (deadline before May 2026)
causal-factors.rationale: With only about two months left, whether 1,000 deaths are reached by the end of April depends on March–April fatalities, making the threshold a live possibility.

causal-factors.name: Data consistency and cross-source uncertainty
causal-factors.rationale: Sources largely converge on a similar February figure (roughly 600), but variations in missing data and reporting introduce uncertainty.

causal-factors.name: Pace of Mediterranean deaths in early 2026
causal-factors.rationale: As of late February 2026, about 606 deaths or missing persons had been recorded in the Mediterranean; if this pace continues into March–April, crossing the 1,000 mark before May becomes plausible (AP News, Guardian, UN Geneva briefings, Feb 2026).

causal-factors.name: Historical annual toll context for the Mediterranean
causal-factors.rationale: IOM data show Mediterranean fatalities around the low-to-mid thousands in recent years (e.g., ~2,185 in 2025 and ~2,452 in 2024), so reaching 1,000 by end-April would be consistent with a normal year’s tempo (UN Geneva briefing Feb 2026; Euronews/Guardian context).

causal-factors.name: Seasonal/weather conditions and sea state
causal-factors.rationale: Spring sea conditions can enable more crossings, while January storms contributed to fatalities; the net effect could sustain or elevate the fatality pace into March–April (AP News Feb 2026; Guardian Feb 23, 2026; UN briefing).

causal-factors.name: Rescue capacity and search-and-rescue operations
causal-factors.rationale: IOM and partners have urged stronger SAR and regional cooperation, which could reduce deaths if capacities are expanded and operations are effectively coordinated (UN Geneva briefing, Feb 2026).

causal-factors.name: European policy crackdown on irregular migration
causal-factors.rationale: Tougher migration controls and deterrence policies in Europe may reduce crossings and fatalities, depending on enforcement and smuggling dynamics (Guardian coverage of policy context, Feb 2026).

causal-factors.name: Data reporting and verification uncertainties
causal-factors.rationale: IOM counts depend on verification; ongoing missing/unverified cases and data access issues can shift observed totals up or down, adding uncertainty around fixed thresholds (UN Geneva briefing; 2025 reporting context).

causal-factors.name: Year-to-date Mediterranean mortality pace (through February 2026)
causal-factors.rationale: About 606 deaths or missing in the Mediterranean through February 2026; if March–April sustain that pace, total could exceed 1,000 by end-April, increasing the likelihood of reaching the threshold before May. (AP News, February 2026; The Guardian, February 2026)

causal-factors.name: Seasonal weather and sea-state conditions raising risk
causal-factors.rationale: Rough seas and storms elevate crossing danger and can worsen outcomes; early 2026 reporting points to weather-driven risk factors in the central Mediterranean. (Le Monde, February 2026)

causal-factors.name: Search-and-rescue capacity and policy responses
causal-factors.rationale: Stronger Search-and- Rescue capacity and safer migration pathways could reduce fatalities if implemented effectively. (UN Geneva press briefing, February 27, 2026)

causal-factors.name: Migrant departure pressure from Libya/Tunisia
causal-factors.rationale: Higher departure flows from North Africa correlate with higher Mediterranean fatalities; 2025 data show substantial migratory movement from Libya/Tunisia. (The Guardian, February 23, 2026)

causal-factors.name: Data reporting gaps and unverified/missing at-sea data
causal-factors.rationale: IOM missing data and verification gaps—e.g., an estimated 1,500 missing at sea in 2025—mean the 2026 toll could be undercounted. (UN Geneva press briefing, February 27, 2026)

synthesis: The objections flag plausible downside risks to surpassing 1,000 Mediterranean deaths by end-April, but the February pace keeps the threshold within reach. A modest downward recalibration is warranted to reflect these uncertainties while preserving the ensemble's informative value.
